summary: Streaming request timeouts during peak load correlated with TP replicas (Dedicated / Acme AI)
description:
Issue summary
- Acme AI reports intermittent streaming timeouts during peak load. Failures present as:
  - client-side disconnects / timeouts while stream is active
  - increased 504s from gateway for streaming routes
  - p99 latency spikes and elevated cancellations
- Correlation: failures concentrate on multi-GPU tensor-parallel (TP) replicas (TP=4) and are much less frequent on single-GPU replicas.

Customer impact
- Customer-facing chat streams terminate mid-response during traffic bursts.
- Acme AI reports ~2–6% of streaming requests timing out between 30–90 seconds during peak.
- Downstream: retries amplify load; user-visible degradation; occasional backlog buildup in their app.

Environment
- Deployment: Dedicated (Acme AI)
- Region: us-east
- GPU: A100 80GB (multi-GPU replicas)
- Runtime: 1.18.x (exact build to confirm from /health/version)
- Mode: streaming chat completions, mixed prompt lengths (short + long), bursty concurrency

What we’re seeing (Redwood side)
- Gateway logs: elevated 504/499 on streaming endpoints during peak windows.
- Runtime logs: decode progress stops for a subset of TP replicas while process stays alive; no hard NCCL error surfaced to API layer in many cases (silent stall signature).
- Dashboard correlation: request timeouts line up with TP heartbeat gaps / in-flight collective counters not progressing on the same replica(s).

Steps to reproduce (customer + internal)
Customer-provided (approx):
1) Sustain concurrency against streaming endpoint (chat) with a mix of prompts:
   - ~70% short prompts (0.5–2k tokens input)
   - ~30% long prompts (6–16k tokens input)
2) Enable streaming and keep client connections open.
3) Drive load in bursts (e.g., ramp to peak over ~2–3 min, hold 10–15 min).
4) Observe a subset of streams stall mid-response and then time out client-side.

Internal repro (in progress):
- Attempting to reproduce with benchmark-lab mixed prefill/decode workload (TP=4) using long-context + bursty concurrency. See ENG initiative for repro harness and perf-canary tasks.

Current mitigation / workaround (in place)
- Concurrency cap (recommended and applied as of 2025-02-20):
  - Reduce max concurrent streaming requests per replica.
  - Practical starting point: cut in half (e.g., 24 -> 12) for TP=4 replicas.
  - Goal: reduce scheduler pressure and likelihood of collective starvation/stall.
- Optional secondary mitigations (if still seeing timeouts):
  - Cap long-context requests (route long prompts to non-TP pool if available, or enforce lower max_input_tokens during peak).
  - Reduce max_batch_tokens to avoid prefill-heavy batches during peak.

Notes / hypotheses
- This is likely the same family as the TP hang signatures under sustained mixed prefill/decode load (scheduler starvation + NCCL collective ordering/stream sync boundary).
- Engineering is actively landing: heartbeat metrics + stall reason codes, scheduler guardrails, NCCL stream/event sync hardening, and TP watchdog/abort semantics (feature-flagged) targeted for runtime 1.19.

Asks / next data needed
- From Acme AI:
  - Client timeout thresholds and any load balancer idle timeout settings.
  - Request IDs for 10–20 failed streams + timestamps (UTC) for correlation.
  - Confirmation of their peak concurrency and prompt length distribution.
- From Redwood SRE/Eng:
  - Confirm affected runtime version(s) and replica topology.
  - Validate whether TP heartbeat gap and collective counters plateau for the same time window.

Next steps
- Keep concurrency cap in place during peak.
- Enable additional NCCL/runtime debug logging for a short canary window if needed (see INT-2219), with careful performance/security review.
- Track fixes in ENG-4821 initiative; plan canary of runtime 1.19.x to Acme AI Dedicated once gating metrics look good.

Owner
- Support owner: Liam O’Rourke
- Eng escalation: Noah Patel / Hiro Tanaka / Sofia Ivanova (Serving Runtime)
- SRE point: Rafael Mendes
comments: 2025-02-19 09:12 PST — Owen Phillips (Support) — Ticket created from customer report in #support-escalations. Customer seeing streaming timeouts during peak; suspected correlation with TP replicas. Looping in Liam (TAM) + Rachel (CS) for comms, and tagging runtime/SRE for triage.

2025-02-19 10:03 PST — Liam O'Rourke (Support/TAM) — Spoke with Acme AI (via Slack Connect). They report 30–90s stream timeouts, mainly during 9–11am PT peak. They can provide request IDs + timestamps. Asked them to share client timeout settings and whether any upstream ALB idle timeout is 60s (common culprit).

2025-02-19 10:36 PST — Aisha Bello (SRE) — Checked tp-stall-and-timeout dashboard for Acme us-east. There’s a clear correlation between request_timeout spikes and tp_rank_heartbeat gaps on 2 replicas in the pool. No matching NCCL error spikes; looks like silent stall. Suggest applying concurrency cap immediately while eng continues fixes.

2025-02-19 11:05 PST — Rafael Mendes (SRE) — +1 on mitigation. We can also temporarily reduce max_batch_tokens and avoid long-context in same pool during peak. If customer approves, we can run a controlled logging window (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO + limited scope) per INT-2219, but we should do it after applying caps to avoid compounding latency.

2025-02-19 12:22 PST — Liam O'Rourke (Support/TAM) — Customer confirmed their client timeout is 75s and upstream LB idle timeout is 120s, so this doesn’t look like a simple idle timeout. They shared 15 request IDs (attached in internal note) that timed out; timestamps align with heartbeat gaps SRE flagged.

2025-02-20 08:41 PST — Liam O'Rourke (Support/TAM) — Coordinated with SRE to apply interim workaround: reduced max concurrent streaming requests per TP replica from 24 -> 12 and lowered max_batch_tokens during peak window. Customer notified this is temporary pending runtime fixes; asked them to monitor %timeouts and report back.

2025-02-20 14:10 PST — Jacob Stein (SRE) — After caps, timeout rate down from ~4% peak to ~0.7% peak (still above baseline). Heartbeat gaps reduced but not eliminated. Suggest keeping caps + proceed with eng instrumentation rollout so we can classify stall reason (compute vs comms vs scheduler).

2025-02-21 09:18 PST — Noah Patel (Eng, Runtime) — This matches the TP stall signature we’re prioritizing in ENG-4821. We have PRs in flight for heartbeat + stall reason codes (21834) and scheduler guardrail for collective starvation (21841). Once 21834 lands, we should be able to tag these stalls more precisely and decide whether to flip watchdog (21860) for Dedicated canary.

2025-02-25 16:02 PST — Rachel Kim (CS) — Customer update: caps helped materially; they’re okay with reduced throughput during peak as long as streaming remains stable. They want an ETA for a permanent fix and would like to be first canary for 1.19 in Dedicated if risk is acceptable.

2025-03-03 11:27 PST — Liam O'Rourke (Support/TAM) — Shared tentative plan with Acme AI: Dedicated-first canary of runtime 1.19.x once gating checks pass. For now, we’re leaving concurrency caps in place. Keeping ticket open until we complete canary + confirm timeouts return to baseline without caps.
